Preach the Word
PREECH thuh WURD
verb phrase (ministry)
From preach, Latin praedicare, to proclaim publicly, rendering Greek kerusso, to herald; the herald cries the word of his King.

📖 Biblical Definition

Preach the word is the dying charge of Paul to Timothy and the standing commission of every pastor. In his last letter the apostle solemnly binds his son in the faith: "I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom; Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Tim 4:1–2). The verb is kerusso, to herald — the preacher is not a lecturer offering opinions but a herald crying the King's decree, and the content is fixed: "the word," the inspired Scripture, not the herald's own wit. Paul foresees the reason for so urgent a charge: "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears" (2 Tim 4:3). The remedy for itching ears is not a different message but the faithful one, pressed in season and out, with reproof, rebuke, and exhortation. This is expository fidelity — the opening and applying of the text — over against entertainment, felt-need talks, and the marketing of the pulpit to consumer appetite. This dictionary confesses that preaching is the heralded word of God, and that a church starved of it, however entertained, is famished.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Paul's solemn charge to herald the inspired Scripture in season and out, with reproof, rebuke, and exhortation. It establishes expository fidelity to the text against entertainment and felt-need preaching.

expand to see more

PREACH THE WORD, verb phrase. To herald the inspired Scripture as the fixed content of the pulpit.

The dying charge of Paul to Timothy, sworn before God and the judging Christ (2 Tim 4:1).

"Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Tim 4:2).

It requires the herald's urgency and the text's authority, against the lectures of mere opinion.

It forbids the trading of the word for entertainment to please itching ears (2 Tim 4:3).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Tim 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

2 Tim 4:1 — "I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom;"

2 Tim 4:3 — "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;"

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Preaching is corrupted wherever the herald's fixed word is swapped for entertainment, felt-need talks, and consumer-driven content designed to soothe rather than to reprove and exhort.

expand to see more

The market church has rebuilt the pulpit around the listener's appetite. Topical talks address felt needs, stories and stagecraft replace exposition, and the sermon is engineered to be inoffensive and brief. This is precisely the apostasy Paul predicted: a generation that "will not endure sound doctrine" and gathers teachers to scratch its "itching ears" (2 Tim 4:3). The error is not in clear communication but in the surrender of the content — "the word" — to the hearer's wishes. A herald who softens the King's decree to keep the crowd has ceased to herald.

The recovery is expository fidelity: to open the text, declare its meaning, and press its reproof, rebuke, and exhortation upon the conscience "with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Tim 4:2). Faith comes by hearing the word (Rom 10:17), and souls are fed and saved by the heralded Scripture, not by performance. The pulpit is therefore to be reformed back to the word — in season when it is welcome, out of season when it is not.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase rests on the verb kerusso, to herald, and on the object "the word," the inspired Scripture proclaimed.

expand to see more

Greek kerusso, to herald, pictures the public crier announcing his king's decree.

The noun keryx, herald, marks the preacher's office as proclamation, not opinion.

"The word," Greek logos, fixes the content as the inspired Scripture, not the speaker's wit.

Latin praedicare, to proclaim before, gives our English preach and predicate.

Instant renders ephistemi, to stand ready upon — the herald always at his post.

Usage

"Charged to preach the word, he opened the text rather than telling stories to fill the hour."

"When the people would not endure sound doctrine, he obeyed the charge to preach the word the more."

"To preach the word is to herald the King's decree, in season and out, whether it is welcomed or refused."
